notes.gunnuma: J’ai mal à la… for a feminine body part: J’ai mal à la tête.
notes.lunnuma: J’ai mal au… for a masculine body part: J’ai mal au ventre.
notes.ndi-mulwadde: A woman says it the same way: Je suis malade.
notes.omusawo: Le médecin, also le docteur. For a woman: la médecin.
notes.nimepona: A woman writes guérie; it sounds the same.

guidebook.intro: Name the parts of the body and say what hurts. French uses “the” where English says “my”, and “I have pain at the head”.

tips.title: J’ai mal à la tête
body: To say what hurts, use **avoir mal à**: **J’ai mal à la tête** (my head hurts), literally “I have pain at the head”. **À** joins with **le** and **les**: **J’ai mal au ventre, j’ai mal aux yeux.**
French uses **la, le, les** for body parts, not **mon, ma**: **J’ai mal au bras**, not “à mon bras”.

tips.title: Being ill
body: **Je suis malade** (I’m ill) uses **être**, like English. Illnesses use **avoir**: **J’ai la grippe** (I have the flu), **J’ai de la fièvre** (I have a fever).
To wish someone well: **Bon rétablissement !** (get well soon) and **Repose-toi** (rest).

tips.title: Œil, yeux
body: Some nouns have irregular plurals: **un œil, des yeux** (eye, eyes). Many words ending in **-al** change to **-aux**: **un hôpital, des hôpitaux**.
**Le bras** (arm) and **le nez** (nose) already end in **s** or **z**, so they don’t change in the plural.

culture.title: Pharmacies
body: In French-speaking cities, a green cross marks **la pharmacie**. Pharmacists give advice and can often help with small problems before you see **le médecin**.
